> This guide is the English version of
> [10. Perfilar una base](perfilar-una-base.html). `lupa` writes its messages
> and tables in Spanish, so the output below is in Spanish.

There is a sales table in a database, perhaps too large for the memory of the
session. How is it decided what the engine computes and how many rows reach R,
and where is it recorded how they were chosen?

> **In this guide:**
>
> - profiling a table with `perfilar_dbi()` and telling apart its 2 blocks,
>   `resumen_tabla` and `perfil_muestra`;
> - comparing what each option brings into R: the default call, `muestra = n`,
>   `universo = "muestra_motor"` and `bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados"`;
> - finding the sampling metadata, which lives in 2 places depending on the
>   option;
> - reading the result with the same accessors as a profile in memory.

## A table in a database

The example uses SQLite in memory, with the packages `DBI` and `RSQLite`. The
table has 1,000 rows so that the guide runs in seconds; the decisions are the
same with millions. `DBI::dbWriteTable()` only prepares the example.
`perfilar_dbi()` (*profile through DBI*) sends read queries: it does not write
to the database or create temporary tables.

```{r tabla, eval = TRUE}
library(lupa)

n <- 1000
ventas <- data.frame(
  id_venta = seq_len(n),
  sucursal = rep(c("Norte", "Sur", "Este", "Oeste"), length.out = n),
  monto = 100 + (seq_len(n) * 37) %% 800,
  fecha = format(as.Date("2026-01-01") + seq_len(n) %% 180),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ventas$monto[seq(7, n, by = 50)] <- NA
head(ventas, 3)
```

```{r conexion}
conexion <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(conexion, "ventas", ventas)
```

## Profiling with the default values

```{r omision}
completo <- perfilar_dbi(conexion, "ventas")
completo
```

```{r omision-cifras, include=FALSE}
lectura_completo <- completo$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo
celdas_tope <- lectura_completo$max_celdas_muestra
mib_tope <- lectura_completo$max_bytes_muestra / 1024^2
stopifnot(
  identical(completo$resumen_tabla$meta$universo, "tabla_completa"),
  lectura_completo$filas_obtenidas == n,
  is.null(completo$resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo)
)
```

The printout shows the 2 blocks:

- «Resumen de tabla completa» is `resumen_tabla` (*table summary*): aggregates
  that the engine computes in SQL over all the rows.
- «Perfil de muestra» is `perfil_muestra` (*sample profile*): `perfilar()` run
  in R on the rows that were read.

The spill lines only have content in PostgreSQL.

By default, `universo = "tabla_completa"` (*universe = whole table*) and
`muestra = Inf` (*sample*). That means:

- the aggregates go through the whole table;
- `lupa` also brings into R **every row that fits within the read caps**. The
  caps are `max_celdas_muestra`
  (`r chartr(".,", ",.", cifra(celdas_tope))` cells by default) and
  `max_bytes_muestra` (`r chartr(".,", ",.", cifra(mib_tope))` MiB).

With this table, all 1,000 rows fit. The default call is not a cheap sample: it
is the whole table, if it fits.

## What each option brings into R

The other 3 decisions are tried on the same table. The result has one row per
option, with:

- how many rows the SQL summary describes;
- how many were read into R;
- in which of the 2 places the sampling metadata was left.

```{r opciones}
acotado <- perfilar_dbi(conexion, "ventas", muestra = 200, orden_muestra = "id_venta")
en_motor <- perfilar_dbi(
  conexion, "ventas", universo = "muestra_motor", muestra_motor = 150
)
agregados <- perfilar_dbi(conexion, "ventas", bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados")

que_trae <- function(perfil, opcion) {
  muestreo_sql <- perfil$resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo
  muestreo_r <- perfil$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo
  data.frame(
    opcion = opcion,
    filas_resumen = if (is.null(muestreo_sql)) {
      n_filas(perfil)
    } else {
      muestreo_sql$filas_obtenidas
    },
    filas_en_r = if (is.null(muestreo_r)) 0 else muestreo_r$filas_obtenidas,
    meta_resumen = !is.null(muestreo_sql),
    meta_lectura = !is.null(muestreo_r)
  )
}

rbind(
  que_trae(completo, "por omisión"),
  que_trae(acotado, "muestra = 200"),
  que_trae(en_motor, "universo = \"muestra_motor\""),
  que_trae(agregados, "bloque_muestra = \"solo_agregados\"")
)
```

```{r opciones-cifras, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  acotado$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo$filas_obtenidas == 200,
  acotado$resumen_tabla$meta$filas == n,
  en_motor$resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo$filas_obtenidas == 150,
  en_motor$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo$filas_obtenidas == 150,
  is.null(agregados$perfil_muestra),
  is.null(acotado$resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo)
)
```

Each row answers a different question (`por omisión` is the default call):

- **`muestra = n`** bounds the read into R, not the aggregates: the summary
  still describes the 1,000 rows, and the row-level profile, 200.
- **`universo = "muestra_motor"`** (*engine sample*) with `muestra_motor = n`
  changes the universe of the aggregates. The engine chooses the sample only
  once and `lupa` keeps it in a copy in the R session. Everything else is
  computed on those same rows: summary and profile describe the same 150.
- **`bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados"`** (*sample block = aggregates only*)
  brings no rows: `perfil_muestra` stays `NULL` and there are only counts and
  summaries computed in the engine. It works for both universes.

`n_filas()` (*number of rows*) always returns the count of the whole table,
also with `muestra_motor`.

## Where the sampling is written down

The last 2 columns of the table above say whether each place where the sampling
metadata lives exists:

- `meta_resumen` looks at `resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo`;
- `meta_lectura` looks at `perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo`.

Each one exists under its own condition:

| path | describes | exists when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo` | the rows read into R | there is a `perfil_muestra`, with any universe |
| `resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo` | the sample chosen by the engine | `universo = "muestra_motor"`; otherwise it is `NULL` |

For the read into R, the metadata says:

- how many rows were requested and how many arrived;
- how many the table has;
- how they were chosen;
- whether the choice can be repeated.

```{r ruta-lectura}
lectura <- acotado$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo
str(lectura[c(
  "filas_solicitadas", "filas_obtenidas", "filas_totales_fuente", "metodo",
  "reproducible"
)])
```

`reproducible` is `TRUE` because `orden_muestra = "id_venta"` (*sample order*)
was declared and `lupa` checked on the whole table that this order is unique.
Without a declared order, a `LIMIT` has no guaranteed order. Then
`reproducible` is `FALSE`, as in the default call:

```{r sin-orden}
sin_orden <- completo$perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo
sin_orden$reproducible
writeLines(strwrap(sin_orden$motivo_reproducibilidad, 88))
```

For the engine sample, the metadata is in the summary. The method depends on
what the engine accepts. `lupa` first tries the variants of `TABLESAMPLE`. If
none works, it orders by a pseudorandom function with the limit of the dialect,
as in SQLite.

```{r ruta-motor}
del_motor <- en_motor$resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo
str(del_motor[c("metodo", "tamano_muestra", "fraccion", "universo", "reproducible")])
```

There `universo` is the size of the table the sample came from, and `fraccion`
(*fraction*) the part that was taken. The pseudorandom sample changes on every
run, and `reproducible` says so. Each metric of `resumen_tabla$sql` also
declares its scope: the row count is from the whole table and the rest, from
the sample.

```{r sql-motor}
sql <- en_motor$resumen_tabla$sql
sql[sql$columna == "monto", c("columna", "metrica", "estado", "alcance")][1:6, ]
```

The status `observado_muestra` (*observed in the sample*) warns that the value
describes the sample. In particular, `n_distintos` is the cardinality observed
in those 150 rows, not an estimate of the cardinality of the table.

## The 2 blocks, side by side {#the-two-blocks-side-by-side}

```{r bloques}
data.frame(
  bloque = c("resumen_tabla", "perfil_muestra"),
  calculado_en = c("el motor", "R"),
  filas = c(n_filas(acotado), n_filas(acotado$perfil_muestra)),
  campos_analiticos = c(
    ncol(acotado$resumen_tabla$columnas) - 1L,
    ncol(acotado$perfil_muestra$columnas) - 1L
  )
)
```

```{r bloques-cifras, include=FALSE}
campos_resumen <- ncol(acotado$resumen_tabla$columnas) - 1L
campos_muestra <- ncol(acotado$perfil_muestra$columnas) - 1L
```

The summary has `r chartr(".,", ",.", cifra(campos_resumen))` analytic fields
per column. They are the ones SQL can compute without bringing the data:
missing values, distinct values, mode, minimum, maximum, mean, median and
standard deviation, among others. The profile of the sample has the
`r chartr(".,", ",.", cifra(campos_muestra))` of `perfilar()`, but on the rows
that were read. That is why `lupa` does not mix them. Calling the summary a
*profile* would claim a completeness it does not have; reading the profile as
if it were of the whole table, too.

## Reading the result with the accessors

The accessors of [Leer un perfil](leer-un-perfil.html) (*Reading a profile*, in
Spanish) work the same on the result of `perfilar_dbi()`. `columnas()`
(*columns*) returns the summary of the engine and `hallazgos()` (*findings*),
the findings of the sample profile:

```{r accesores}
columnas(acotado)[, c("columna", "n", "n_faltantes", "n_distintos", "minimo", "maximo")]
hallazgos(acotado)[, c("columna", "tipo_hallazgo", "severidad", "n_afectados")]
nrow(sql_perfil(acotado))
```

The engine counted the `r chartr(".,", ",.", cifra(sum(is.na(ventas$monto))))`
missing values of `monto` in the 1,000 rows. In its 200 rows, the row-level
profile found that:

- `fecha` is stored as text although it holds dates
  (`tipo_declarado_distinto`, *declared type differs*);
- almost every row carries a different date (`alta_cardinalidad`, *high
  cardinality*).

`sql_perfil()` (*SQL profile*) returns one row per column and metric, with the
query that produced it, its status and its reason.

When the sample was not requested, the accessors do not make up what is not
there:

- `hallazgos()` returns an empty table with a warning;
- `cobertura()` (*coverage*) declares the block as `no_solicitado` (*not
  requested*), which is not a failure.

```{r sin-muestra}
aviso <- NULL
sin_filas <- withCallingHandlers(
  hallazgos(agregados),
  warning = function(w) {
    aviso <<- conditionMessage(w)
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
nrow(sin_filas)
writeLines(strwrap(aviso, 88))
cobertura(agregados)[, c("bloque", "elemento", "estado")]
```

## ⚠️ What the summary does not guarantee {#what-the-summary-does-not-guarantee}

The aggregates are separate queries, and the table can change between one and
the next. The summary declares it:

```{r snapshot}
completo$resumen_tabla$meta$snapshot
writeLines(strwrap(completo$resumen_tabla$meta$nota_snapshot, 88))
```

If `n_validos` and `n_distintos` come out inconsistent and come from different
queries, `cobertura()` adds an `alcance_distinto` (*different scope*) row with
the 2 statements. It is evidence that the table changed during the run, not an
accusation against the engine.

## Before connecting to another engine

The engine package and the system library underneath are installed by whoever
uses `lupa`. The error that shows up when one of them is missing rarely says
which. `requisitos_motor()` (*engine requirements*) says it before connecting:

```{r requisitos, eval = FALSE}
requisitos_motor()            # the whole catalog
requisitos_motor("mariadb")   # what MariaDB needs and how to get it
```

For each engine it returns:

- the R package;
- the system library, with its name in Debian and in Fedora;
- the way to install it without administrator rights, when there is one;
- the expected dialect;
- the testing status of the engine.

## ⏱ For a large table {#for-a-large-table}

Before profiling a table of millions of rows, it pays to look at the plan.
`plan_perfilado_dbi()` (*DBI profiling plan*) counts the queries and the work
that `perfilar_dbi()` would do with the same arguments, without reading data.
The guide [Engines and scale](engines-and-scale.html) gathers what is needed
to decide:

- the cost of each metric and the batches of queries;
- the cost policy;
- the memory budgets;
- the copy of the sample that the session keeps;
- the dialects;
- the guarantee of the primary key depending on the engine;
- the matrix of tested engines.

```{r cierre-conexion}
DBI::dbDisconnect(conexion)
```

## Summary

- `perfilar_dbi()` returns 2 blocks: `resumen_tabla`, computed in the engine,
  and `perfil_muestra`, computed in R on the rows that were read.
- By default the aggregates cover the whole table. The row-level profile, also
  by default, brings every row that fits within the read caps.
- `muestra = n` bounds the read into R; `universo = "muestra_motor"` samples in
  the engine; `bloque_muestra = "solo_agregados"` brings no rows.
- The sampling of what was read is in `perfil_muestra$meta$origen_dbi$muestreo`;
  the one of the engine, in `resumen_tabla$meta$muestreo`, only with
  `muestra_motor`.
- `meta$snapshot = FALSE`: the aggregates are not an instantaneous reading.
